newsitem.title: BELGIUM: MEPs attacks failings of EU structural funds.
newsitem.headline: MEPs attacks failings of EU structural funds.

text.p: The Structural Funds, which account for nearly a third of the EU's budget, are fiendishly complex to use, not properly targeted or coordinated and seriously underspent, a British Liberal MEP said on Tuesday.

The structure and administration of the funds is so complex that the majority of European Union citizens and potential beneficiaries find them incomprehensible, Robin Teverson, the author of a European Parliament report on the use of the funds in 1994, told Reuters.

In addition, clear aims and targets for the funds, in terms of narrowing the gap in GDP between different regions of the EU or creating sustainable jobs, for example, were conspicuous by their absence, Teverson complained.
This made it very difficult for either the European Commission or the parliament to assess the performance of the funds, he added.

Teverson's report, which he will present to the parliament's plenary session in Brussels on Wednesday, uses as its starting point the Commission's sixth annual report on the structural funds (1994) - COM(95)583.
Teverson said he welcomed the substantial amount of money - 141 billion ecus - allocated to the funds for the period 1994-1999.
But he voiced concern about the level of underspending in 1994 and the Commission's failure to keep tabs on the money after it had been sent to the member states' governments.

Under the structural funds' rules, the member states are obliged to match Ecu for Ecu the amount contributed by the EU. But at the moment, cash-strapped governments are trying to prevent EU funds going through rather than honour their part of the deal, Teverson said.

Some 21 billion Ecus were made available to member states through the funds in 1994. The Commission's report gives details of the percentage paid out to the national governments but the EU executive has no comprehensive information on when the money actually arrives in the regions and when the projects are implemented.
"It could, as is often the case in the UK, be just sitting in the Chancellor's bank account keeping down the public sector borrowing requirement," the Liberal MEP said.

Another of the MEP's complaints is the absence of projects which involve regions in more than one member state. Bureaucratic complexities mean the potential for a truly European approach is squandered, he said.

Finally, there was sadly little coordination between the funds - the major financial tool for implementing EU regional policy - and the EU's main strategies for developing the Union's regions and protecting the environment, he complained.
This said, Teverson insisted the structural funds had an important role to play in reducing the economic and social disparities between Europe's regions.
He said he was pleased the Commission had begun to accept the need to simplify the way the funds worked.

And he suggested other improvements were possible before the current funds expire in 1999, such as gleaning more information on what the member states did with the money, stepping up cooperation between different regions and easing the cash flow problems affecting small firms and voluntary organisations wanting to participate in the projects.
"That just takes political will," he concluded.
